title: Patterns & Sequences
coreInsight: A sequence is generated by structure; good pattern reasoning identifies what remains consistent rather than merely guessing the next visible term.
targetLearnerRealization: A few terms do not define a pattern; a useful sequence rule explains how every term is generated and distinguishes recursive from positional structure.
learningObjectives: Explain why a short list of terms does not uniquely determine a sequence.
Keep term index separate from term value.
Generate terms from a stated recursive rule.
Evaluate terms from an explicit rule and translate simple arithmetic sequences between forms.
Recognize arithmetic, non-arithmetic, and repeating sequence structures.

continuity.openingCallback: Use numerical structure to test whether a proposed continuation is reasonable, then ask whether reasonableness proves uniqueness.
closingSeeds: A stated rule, not a short prefix, defines how a sequence continues.
Recursive rules use earlier terms while explicit rules use the term position directly.
Repeating sequences can be indexed through cycle position.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Every sequence has a constant difference.
The term number and the term value are the same quantity.
A few matching terms prove a guessed rule.
Recursive and explicit descriptions are interchangeable without translation.

beats.purpose: Expose non-uniqueness by asking what a short prefix logically forces.
beats.expectedRealization: Several rules can fit 1, 2, 4 and produce different next terms.
beats.transitionIn: A sequence beginning 1, 2, 4 invites a quick guess. Before extending it, decide what the visible terms actually prove.
beats.whyNow: The deliberately ambiguous prefix directly surfaces the lesson's central misconception before any sequence vocabulary is named.
beats.entryBridge: Treat each proposed continuation as a claim that needs a rule, not as a visual reflex.
beats.exitBridge: Different valid rules explain the same three terms, so the rule itself is essential information.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Term cards labeled by position, followed by alternative rule cards.
learnerPrompts: Can two precise rules agree on the first three terms but disagree on the fourth?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. No next term is guaranteed until a rule is stated.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Try “double each term” and “add 1, then 2, then 3.” Both fit 1, 2, 4 but give different fourth terms.

visual.ariaLabel: Two precise sequence rules agreeing on one two four but continuing with eight and seven

steps.title: Construct two continuations
steps.body: Doubling gives 8 next. Increasing by +1, +2, then +3 gives 7 next.

steps.title: Use the disagreement
steps.body: Because both rules fit every shown term, the prefix alone cannot force one answer.

resolution.takeaway: A few terms suggest patterns; a stated rule defines the sequence.

beats.purpose: Shift attention from next-term guessing to complete generation rules.
beats.expectedRealization: A useful rule specifies how to generate every relevant term.
beats.transitionIn: The fourth term became knowable only when a rule card was attached. Decide which description is precise enough to run.
beats.prompt: Which statement completely defines a continuation after the starting term 3?

options.text: Each later term is twice the previous term plus 1.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. It names a repeatable action and the earlier value it uses.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A complete rule must determine each later term, not merely describe a trend or guess one value.

steps.title: Run the definition
steps.body: Starting at 3, the rule produces 7, then 15, then 31. At every step the previous term determines the next.

resolution.takeaway: A sequence rule must be precise enough to generate terms consistently.

beats.purpose: Separate position labels from the numerical values stored at those positions.
beats.expectedRealization: Term number identifies a slot; term value is the number in that slot.
beats.transitionIn: Rules fill a chain of positions. Keep each position label separate from the value written on its card.
beats.prompt: The sequence cards are #1 → 5, #2 → 8, #3 → 11, #4 → 14. Which statement is true?

options.text: The fourth term must have value 4.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The index is 4; the value occupying that position is 14.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Read each card as “position number → stored value.” Do not swap the two roles.

visual.ariaLabel: Four term cards with separate position labels and values

steps.title: Name both quantities
steps.body: The index counts where the card sits. The term value is the number generated for that card.

resolution.takeaway: Term number and term value are different quantities.

beats.purpose: Compare recursive and explicit descriptions of the same arithmetic sequence.
beats.expectedRealization: A recursive rule advances from a previous term; an explicit rule jumps directly from index to value.
beats.transitionIn: The cards 5, 8, 11, 14 rise by 3. Describe the same structure in two different ways.
beats.prompt: Which pair correctly describes 5, 8, 11, 14, ... both recursively and explicitly?

options.text: Recursive: start 5 and add 3; explicit: a_n = 5 + 3(n - 1).
Recursive: a_n = 5 + 3(n - 1); explicit: look at the previous term.
Both descriptions must use exactly the same words.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. One walks from card to card; the other uses the index to jump directly.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The recursive form must name a starting term and how to get the next; the explicit form must use n directly.

visual.ariaLabel: Recursive and explicit descriptions of the same arithmetic sequence

steps.title: Check the translation
steps.body: From term 1 to term n there are n - 1 additions of 3, so 5 + 3(n - 1) reaches the same value.

resolution.takeaway: Recursive rules use earlier terms; explicit rules use position.

beats.purpose: Name sequence, term, recursive rule, explicit rule, and arithmetic sequence after discovery.
beats.expectedRealization: The vocabulary distinguishes position, value, and two ways of generating structure.
beats.name: Sequence rules
beats.conciseDefinition: A sequence is an ordered list generated by a rule. A recursive rule builds from earlier terms; an explicit rule gives a term from its index. An arithmetic sequence has one constant difference between consecutive terms.
beats.formalization: recursive: a_n from earlier terms · explicit: a_n from n · arithmetic: a_n = a_1 + d(n - 1)
beats.memoryHook: State the rule; label the position; generate, don't guess.

beats.purpose: Apply a clearly stated three-term recursive rule while keeping feeder terms, index, and value distinct.
beats.expectedRealization: Each new term depends on the previous three values, and the eighth term is a value, not the number 8.
beats.transitionIn: The opening prefix was ambiguous because no rule was given. This contest sequence states exactly which earlier terms feed each new one.
beats.whyNow: The learner can now trust a stated recurrence and track term positions separately from their generated values.
beats.entryBridge: Write each new value on its numbered card, then slide the three-term window one card right.
beats.exitBridge: The recurrence produces one unique eighth value because every feeder choice is specified.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Numbered term cards with arrows from the prior three cards into the new card.
learnerPrompts: Which three seed values begin the sequence?
Which three cards feed term 8, and what value do they produce?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Terms 5, 6, and 7 are 11, 20, and 37, so term 8 is 68.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Generate one card at a time, always summing the three immediately before the empty card.

resolution.takeaway: A precise recursive rule makes every later term determined, even when the differences are not constant.

beats.purpose: Reject the assumption that every sequence has constant difference.
beats.expectedRealization: Arithmetic is one specific structure, not a synonym for sequence.
beats.transitionIn: The three-term-sum sequence grew without a constant difference. Compare it with a genuinely arithmetic list.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compute consecutive differences. Arithmetic requires the same difference every time.

steps.title: Check all shown gaps
steps.body: For 4, 9, 14, 19, each gap is 5. The other lists follow rules too, but their differences are not constant.

resolution.takeaway: Every arithmetic sequence is a sequence; not every sequence is arithmetic.

beats.purpose: Assess an arithmetic term using the number of gaps.
beats.whyNow: Begin practice with a direct constant-difference structure.
beats.entryBridge: Count steps from term 1 to term 12, not twelve additions.
beats.exitBridge: Eleven equal gaps connect the first and twelfth cards.
learnerPrompts: How many differences lie between term 1 and term 12?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Eleven additions of 4 take 7 to 51.
beats.incorrectFeedback: There are 12 terms but only 11 gaps after the first term.

steps.title: Count gaps
steps.body: Term 12 is eleven steps after term 1.

resolution.takeaway: Use n - 1 equal steps from the first term to term n.

beats.purpose: Assess faithful propagation of a recursive rule.
beats.whyNow: Keep the same arithmetic structure but state it recursively.
beats.entryBridge: Write the position beside every generated value.
beats.exitBridge: The sixth card contains 17, separating index from value.
learnerPrompts: What value is produced after five additions beyond the seed?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Start with term 1 equal to 2, then add 3 exactly five times to reach term 6.

resolution.takeaway: A recursive rule advances one indexed card at a time.

beats.whyNow: Switch from walking recursively to jumping directly by index.
beats.entryBridge: Use 15 as the index n, not as a term value already known.
beats.exitBridge: The formula maps index 15 directly to value 43.
learnerPrompts: Which number replaces n in a_15?
beats.incorrectFeedback: The subscript 15 is the term position, so substitute n = 15.

resolution.takeaway: An explicit rule uses the index to reach a term directly.

beats.purpose: Assess a non-arithmetic recurrence with two operations.
beats.whyNow: Remove the constant-difference support while retaining a precise rule.
beats.entryBridge: Apply “double, then add one” to the newest term each time.
beats.exitBridge: The changing gaps confirm that a valid sequence need not be arithmetic.
learnerPrompts: Which previous value feeds each new calculation?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use only the immediately previous term and apply both operations in order.

steps.title: Check the structure
steps.body: The gaps 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 are not constant, so the sequence is not arithmetic.

resolution.takeaway: A precise recursive sequence can have changing differences.

beats.purpose: Assess a far-index term through repeating cycle position.
beats.whyNow: Finish with a positional structure that is neither arithmetic nor generated by growth.
beats.entryBridge: Group the sequence into complete red-blue-green cycles before locating term 100.
beats.exitBridge: The remainder identifies the position inside the next cycle.
learnerPrompts: After 99 tiles, which position in the three-color cycle comes next?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Ninety-nine completes 33 cycles, so tile 100 is red.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Divide 100 by the cycle length 3 and interpret the remainder as a cycle position.

steps.title: Count full cycles
steps.body: 99 = 33(3), so tile 99 completes a green third position.

steps.title: Start the next cycle
steps.body: Tile 100 is position 1 of the next cycle: red.

resolution.takeaway: A repeating rule turns a large term index into a cycle position.

beats.purpose: Consolidate rule sufficiency, index/value separation, and recursive/explicit choices.
beats.expectedRealization: Strong sequence reasoning states and verifies the generator before extrapolating.
beats.transitionIn: Ambiguous prefixes, arithmetic gaps, three-term sums, formulas, and cycles all demanded the same safeguards.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable sequence routine? Select all four.

options.text: State a precise rule instead of assuming a short prefix is unique.
Keep each term's position separate from its value.
Decide whether the rule uses earlier terms, the index, or a repeating cycle.
Verify the proposed rule against every given term and condition.

response.feedback: Each action prevents a different pattern-reading error.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes—define, label, choose the right rule form, and verify.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four matter; a plausible next number is not yet a defined or checked sequence.

visual.ariaLabel: Four safeguards for reasoning about sequences

steps.title: Explain more than one term
steps.body: A useful rule accounts for every given term and determines the requested position without changing meaning halfway through.

resolution.takeaway: Generate from a verified rule; do not merely guess the next visible term.

beats.purpose: Connect repeating sequence structure to future units-digit cycles without assigning an unmapped successor.
beats.expectedRealization: Repeated multiplication can create a short cycle even when the full numbers grow rapidly.
beats.transitionIn: Colors repeated every three positions. Numerical features can repeat too, even when the numbers themselves keep growing.
beats.prompt: The powers of 2 end in 2, 4, 8, 6, then repeat those units digits. How could that four-term cycle reveal the units digit of 2^100 without computing the full power?
beats.takeaway: When a feature repeats, use the term index to locate its position in the cycle.

notes: Design: the opening 1,2,4 prefix supports several incompatible continuations, forcing a move from guessing to explicit rule statements. Numbered term cards then separate index from value and distinguish recursive walking from explicit jumping. The closing carries cycle indexing toward units-digit patterns.

Beat outline: ambiguous-prefix anchor -> precise rule card -> index/value cards -> recursive/explicit translation -> name sequences -> authentic three-term recurrence -> arithmetic contrast -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> units-digit hook.

The authentic animation appears after submission; six prompts align with its seed state and five generated-term states. The term-index label was raised to the shared readability minimum. No new lesson visual primitive was needed.

All generated answers were verified by the stated recurrence or formula and independently through closed forms, alternate descriptions, constructive counterexamples, or cycle remainders. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
